content.Economic Recovery:
‭Afghanistan Humanitarian Crisis: Key Focus‬
‭Areas and Strategies‬
‭Economic Recovery‬
‭Challenges:‬‭Afghanistan’s economy suffered a severe‬‭collapse after the Taliban takeover in August 2021.‬
‭Before the takeover, the country was‬‭75% dependent‬‭on foreign aid‬‭, which funded public salaries and‬
‭services​‬
‭hrw.org‬
‭. When donor support was cut off and‬‭about $9 billion‬‭in Afghan foreign reserves were frozen‬‭abroad​‬
‭hrw.org‬
‭, millions lost their incomes virtually overnight. By early 2024,‬‭approximately 85% of Afghans live‬‭on‬
‭less than one dollar a day‬‭, reflecting widespread‬‭poverty​‬
‭amu.tv‬
‭. The economy has stabilized somewhat at a very low level – the World Bank notes‬‭modest GDP growth‬
‭(~2.7%)‬‭after the initial contraction, but this has‬‭only regained‬‭10%‬‭of the output lost since 2020​‬
‭worldbank.org‬
‭. Economic activity remains hamstrung by‬‭fiscal constraints,‬‭a huge trade deficit, and almost no‬
‭capacity for public investment‬‭​‬
‭worldbank.org‬
‭. With the Taliban government unrecognized, the central bank is cut off from the international system,‬
‭limiting liquidity and foreign trade​file-5qtbsnewp7oqv1u5ouacvj.‬
‭Strategies for Improvement:‬‭Realistic steps to revive‬‭Afghanistan’s economy focus on humanitarian‬
‭relief and basic functionality rather than large-scale development.‬‭Injecting liquidity through‬
‭international aid‬‭is crucial – humanitarian cash programs‬‭and salary payments for essential workers can‬
‭restore some purchasing power​‬
‭hrw.org‬
‭hrw.org‬
‭.‬‭Unlocking frozen assets for strictly humanitarian‬‭uses‬‭is one proposal. For example, funds seized‬
‭from the Afghan central bank could be transferred into U.N.-administered trusts to purchase food and‬
‭medicine, rather than handed to the de facto authorities​file-5qtbsnewp7oqv1u5ouacvj.‬‭Trade initiatives‬
‭can also help: regional countries have maintained commerce with Afghanistan – Iran, for instance, is‬
‭working on port and railway projects (Chabahar port and rail links) and crop substitution to curb the illicit‬
‭economy​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. Supporting such projects could integrate Afghanistan into regional supply chains and provide jobs.‬
‭Economic reforms‬‭under Taliban rule are limited, but some measures have modestly improved revenue‬
‭(e.g. anti-corruption efforts at customs). The‬‭World‬‭Bank emphasizes enabling women’s economic‬
‭participation‬‭and investing in human capital as essential‬‭for any sustained recovery​‬
‭worldbank.org‬
‭. Reversing bans on women workers would immediately expand the labor force and productivity. Slovenia‬
‭can support policies in the UN Security Council (UNSC) that tie any future development assistance or‬
‭sanctions relief to concrete economic reforms – for example, urging the Taliban to reopen banks and‬
‭allow women to work, in exchange for technical support to bolster banking operations. Slovenia could‬
‭also back the creation of a UNSC‬‭“Working Group on‬‭Afghan Economic Recovery”‬‭to coordinate aid,‬
‭infrastructure projects, and advice for Afghanistan’s economy (as Slovenia’s delegation has suggested) to‬
‭ensure international efforts are cohesive.‬
‭Role of International Aid:‬‭International financial‬‭institutions and donors remain cautious but not absent.‬
‭The EU, World Bank, and Asian Development Bank have all crafted mechanisms to aid Afghans without‬
‭legitimizing the Taliban. Slovenia can champion‬‭increased‬‭funding to U.N. agencies and NGOs‬
‭operating in Afghanistan, ensuring that lifesaving assistance also shores up the local economy (for‬
‭instance by hiring local staff and purchasing Afghan produce when possible).‬‭Trade facilitation‬‭is‬
‭another angle – Slovenia and EU partners might support initiatives for duty-free access to Afghan goods‬
‭or corridor projects that connect Afghan traders to global markets. In summary, while full economic‬
‭normalization is unrealistic under the current regime, targeted steps – humanitarian cash infusions,‬
‭regional trade support, and conditional engagement on economic management – can mitigate collapse and‬
‭lay groundwork for future recovery​‬
‭worldbank.org‬
‭. Slovenia should support these pragmatic efforts in line with its commitment to help the Afghan people‬
‭without empowering the Taliban.‬
‭Human and Women’s Rights‬
‭Current Situation:‬‭The human rights landscape in Afghanistan‬‭is dire, with‬‭women and girls bearing‬
‭the brunt of Taliban repression‬‭. Since 2021, the Taliban‬‭have barred girls from secondary and higher‬
‭education and pushed women out of most jobs and public life. It has now been‬‭over 1,100 days‬‭of such‬
‭“blatant abuse and trampling of women’s rights,” as Slovenia’s Foreign Minister Tanja Fajon noted​‬
‭buildingtrust.si‬
‭. The Taliban’s decrees – recently codified into a so-called‬‭morality law‬‭– amount to a‬‭“gender‬
‭apartheid”‬‭, systematically persecuting women for their‬‭gender​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭buildingtrust.si‬
‭. Women are forbidden from school beyond age 12 and cannot work in NGOs, government, many‬
‭industries, or even move freely without a male guardian​‬
‭buildingtrust.si‬
‭. These edicts not only destroy women’s freedoms but also‬‭harm the entire society’s future‬‭, depriving‬
‭Afghanistan of half its talent. Outside of women’s rights, the broader human rights situation is also‬
‭alarming: dissent is crushed, media freedom is curtailed, and there are credible reports of extrajudicial‬
‭killings, especially of former officials and minorities. The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees has‬
‭identified Afghanistan as‬‭“one of the world’s most‬‭urgent crises”‬‭due to‬‭human rights violations,‬
‭economic instability, acute hunger, and natural disasters‬‭– a combination that can threaten regional‬
‭stability​‬
‭reporting.unhcr.org‬
‭.‬
‭International Frameworks and Best Practices:‬‭The international‬‭community has condemned the‬
‭Taliban’s actions and laid out clear expectations. The UNSC unanimously passed‬‭Resolution 2681‬
‭(2023)‬‭, which‬‭“called for a swift reversal of all‬‭restrictions on women’s rights”‬‭in Afghanistan​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. This resolution – supported by Slovenia – sends a strong signal that Taliban policies are unacceptable.‬
‭Moreover, multiple countries (including Slovenia during its September 2024 Security Council presidency)‬
‭have raised the possibility that the Taliban’s gender persecution could constitute crimes against humanity‬
‭under the‬‭Rome Statute of the International Criminal‬‭Court‬‭​‬
‭buildingtrust.si‬
‭. Beyond U.N. resolutions, the‬‭Women, Peace and Security‬‭(WPS)‬‭agenda offers a framework: U.N.‬
‭member states have affirmed that women’s participation is crucial to peace and stability. Slovenia joined a‬
‭joint Security Council stakeout‬‭in 2024 declaring‬‭that‬‭“the future of any country, including Afghanistan,‬
‭cannot be prosperous unless it is inclusive”‬‭and urging‬‭the Taliban to‬‭“immediately end all‬
‭discriminatory practices”‬‭against women and girls​‬
‭buildingtrust.si‬
‭. This reflects best practices of unified diplomatic pressure.‬
‭Successful approaches in other contexts can be applied here. One is sustained‬‭monitoring and reporting‬‭:‬
‭a U.N. Special Rapporteur for Afghanistan’s human rights was appointed and should continue to‬
‭document abuses, keeping global attention and pressure. Another is leveraging influential‬
‭Muslim-majority countries and scholars to challenge the Taliban’s policies on Islamic grounds – for‬
‭instance, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) has called the bans on girls’ education un-Islamic‬
‭and appointed an envoy to engage the Taliban.‬‭Targeted‬‭sanctions‬‭are also a tool: the UNSC can impose‬
‭travel bans or asset freezes on individual Taliban leaders responsible for egregious violations (some such‬
‭sanctions already exist for terrorism reasons). However, care must be taken to avoid harming the‬
‭population; thus, targeted measures coupled with humanitarian carve-outs are best practice. International‬
‭humanitarian organizations, despite restrictions, are finding creative ways to support Afghan women – for‬
‭example,‬‭UNICEF’s “secret schools”‬‭or community-based‬‭education programs allow some girls to keep‬
‭learning quietly. Supporting local‬‭women-led NGOs‬‭(many now operating from exile or underground) is‬
‭another best practice to maintain civil society. Slovenia can advocate these measures in the UNSC: call‬
‭for regular reviews of Taliban’s human rights record, support resolutions that condemn abuses, and ensure‬
‭any engagement with Afghan authorities is conditional on‬‭measurable human rights improvements‬‭. In‬
‭essence, Slovenia’s stance is to be‬‭“the voice of‬‭oppressed women and girls in Afghanistan”‬‭​‬
‭file-5qtbsnewp7oqv1u5ouacvj‬
‭– meaning Slovenia will push the UNSC to prioritize human rights in all decisions on Afghanistan. Only‬
‭by upholding international norms – such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and conventions‬
‭on women’s rights – can there be hope for improving conditions on the ground.‬
‭Immediate Humanitarian Aid‬
‭Urgent Needs:‬‭Afghanistan faces an acute humanitarian‬‭catastrophe. Over‬‭23.7 million people (more‬
‭than half the population) require humanitarian assistance‬‭for basic survival​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. Of these, nearly‬‭15 million suffer acute food insecurity‬‭,‬‭and about‬‭3 million children are acutely‬
‭malnourished or at risk of starvation‬‭​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. The country’s healthcare system is on the brink of collapse – hospitals lack medicines, and many clinics‬
‭that were donor-funded have closed, leaving millions without care. Shelter and water are also critical‬
‭concerns: many Afghans lack adequate housing or clean water, especially displaced families. Years of war‬
‭and recent natural disasters have compounded the crisis. In the winter of 2023–2024,‬‭harsh cold and a‬
‭series of earthquakes (such as the major quakes in Herat province)‬‭left tens of thousands in need of‬
‭emergency shelter​‬
‭amu.tv‬
‭. Meanwhile, a new wave of displacement is occurring: since September 2023,‬‭over 618,000 Afghans‬
‭have returned or been expelled from Pakistan‬‭amid‬‭crackdowns, arriving in Afghanistan often‬
‭homeless and destitute​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. These returnees add to an internally displaced population in need of food, warmth, and jobs. In sum,‬
‭Afghanistan’s immediate needs span‬‭food, healthcare,‬‭nutrition, shelter, clean water, and basic‬
‭supplies‬‭to keep people alive.‬
‭Humanitarian Response:‬‭Despite challenges, humanitarian‬‭organizations are on the ground trying to‬
‭deliver aid. In 2023,‬‭over 28 million Afghans received‬‭some form of assistance‬‭– an enormous effort‬
‭led by the U.N. and NGOs​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. However, funding and access remain problematic. The U.N.’s 2024 Humanitarian Response Plan for‬
‭Afghanistan was only‬‭21% funded as of mid-2024‬‭, causing‬‭agencies like the World Food Programme to‬
‭cut food rations​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. Aid workers also face Taliban-imposed obstacles, notably the‬‭ban on Afghan women working for U.N.‬
‭agencies and NGOs‬‭, which OCHA warns is hampering aid‬‭delivery​‬
‭amu.tv‬
‭. Still, many organizations have found ways to keep operating (often by using male-female “mahram”‬
‭teams or negotiating exceptions in health and education sectors). International and regional actors must‬
‭step up to prevent a complete catastrophe.‬‭Slovenia‬‭and other UNSC members can push for immediate‬
‭measures‬‭: urging donor countries to fully fund the‬‭U.N.’s appeals and‬‭close the $3+ billion funding‬‭gap‬‭​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭, and calling on the Taliban to grant unimpeded access to humanitarian workers of‬‭all genders‬‭. Notably,‬
‭UNSC Resolution 2615 (2021) already carved out humanitarian exceptions to sanctions, allowing aid to‬
‭flow; Slovenia should ensure this exception remains and is strengthened so that fears of legal breaches do‬
‭not impede aid​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭.‬
‭Coordinating Aid Efforts:‬‭A mix of international and‬‭regional initiatives is needed. The U.N. continues‬
‭to lead on humanitarian coordination through its mission (UNAMA) and OCHA, but support from‬
‭neighboring countries is invaluable. Pakistan and Iran host millions of Afghan refugees and have served‬
‭as transit hubs for aid – they will require financial help to keep borders open and assist refugees.‬‭Greater‬
‭responsibility-sharing‬‭is a must: UNHCR emphasizes‬‭that the international community needs to help‬
‭Afghanistan’s neighbors and invest in resilience to prevent further refugee flows​‬
‭reporting.unhcr.org‬
‭reporting.unhcr.org‬
‭. Regional organizations like the‬‭OIC and SAARC‬‭(South‬‭Asian Association) can also play a role in‬
‭mobilizing aid from Muslim-majority nations, which might have more influence with the Taliban.‬
‭Bilaterally, countries like Qatar, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan have delivered food, energy, and medical‬
‭aid directly to Afghanistan; Slovenia can encourage the EU to support and upscale such bilateral efforts.‬
‭One creative approach, as mentioned, is to‬‭use frozen‬‭Afghan assets to purchase relief‬
‭supplies‬‭​file-5qtbsnewp7oqv1u5ouacvj – for example,‬‭using seized central bank funds to buy wheat,‬
‭which can then be distributed through the World Food Programme. This would inject resources without‬
‭handing cash to the Taliban.‬
‭In UNSC discussions,‬‭Slovenia can advocate a humanitarian‬‭“airlift” or corridor system‬‭– akin to‬
‭past operations – to get food and medicine into remote Afghan regions before next winter. Additionally,‬
‭protecting humanitarian workers is crucial: Slovenia should support language that condemns interference‬
‭in aid operations and demands the Taliban‬‭lift the‬‭ban on women aid workers for aid to continue‬‭​‬
‭amu.tv‬
‭. In the immediate term, saving lives is the priority. As Slovenia’s delegation has argued,‬‭“Immediate aid‬
‭must be given to the millions at risk of famine and to the women who have been so deeply oppressed‬
‭under Taliban rule”‬‭​file-5qtbsnewp7oqv1u5ouacvj. This‬‭means food on tables, hospitals running, and safe‬
‭shelters – all achievable if the international community maintains focus and funding despite political‬
‭differences with those in power. Slovenia’s voice in the Council can help keep that focus on the‬
‭humanitarian imperative.‬
‭Engagement with the Taliban‬
‭Backchannel Engagement vs. Recognition:‬‭Navigating‬‭relations with the Taliban is a delicate balancing‬
‭act. Slovenia and the wider international community have explicitly‬‭refused to grant formal recognition‬
‭to the Taliban regime. At the same time, some level of engagement is unavoidable if we are to deliver aid‬
‭and influence behavior. The key is to engage‬‭pragmatically‬‭without legitimizing. As the U.N. Special‬
‭Representative for Afghanistan, Roza Otunbayeva, told the Security Council,‬‭“engagement is not‬
‭normalization”‬‭– talking to the de facto authorities‬‭“does not mean legitimization of the Taliban”‬‭​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. This principle guides current backchannels. For instance, the U.N. has convened a series of‬‭meetings‬‭in‬
‭Doha‬‭(Qatar) where Taliban representatives meet informally‬‭with envoys from various countries. In June‬
‭2024, a third such meeting was held to‬‭“reinforce‬‭the principles underlining the consensus to engage”‬
‭while reiterating that fundamental international expectations (like women’s rights) remain firm​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. These backdoor talks allow dialogue on urgent issues – humanitarian access, security concerns,‬
‭economic stability –‬‭without implying diplomatic recognition‬‭.‬‭Slovenia can support this‬‭Doha process‬
‭and similar initiatives that keep channels open. Another form of low-profile engagement is through‬
‭technical discussions: for example, UNAMA and agencies frequently negotiate with Taliban officials at‬
‭the working level to resolve practical problems (like reopening a clinic or obtaining permission for a UN‬
‭flight). Such‬‭confidence-building measures‬‭can yield‬‭small concessions. A recent example is health and‬
‭education: in some provinces, local Taliban authorities quietly allowed‬‭community schools for girls‬‭or‬
‭permitted women in healthcare roles, due to community pressure and negotiation. Encouraging these local‬
‭exceptions and expanding them could build trust gradually.‬
‭Maintaining Principles:‬‭While engaging, the international‬‭community must hold clear red lines. The‬‭EU‬
‭has laid out five benchmarks‬‭for the Taliban (preventing‬‭terrorism, respecting human rights – especially‬
‭women’s rights – forming an inclusive government, allowing free humanitarian access, and permitting‬
‭freedom of travel for those who wish to leave)​‬
‭aa.com.tr‬
‭aa.com.tr‬
‭. Slovenia aligns with this approach: any deeper cooperation depends on Taliban actions. In practice, this‬
‭means any backchannel contacts should‬‭consistently‬‭reiterate demands‬‭such as reopening girls’ schools‬
‭or ending punitive policies, even if immediate change is unlikely. Small‬‭confidence-building steps‬‭could‬
‭be pursued: for instance, if the Taliban were to rescind one or two restrictions (say, allowing women to‬
‭work in humanitarian operations), international actors could respond with a modest concession of their‬
‭own, like unfreezing a small amount of funds for salaries or providing additional relief in that area. These‬
‭step-by-step gestures‬‭build confidence without ever‬‭compromising on core principles. It’s a strategy of‬
‭incremental reciprocity, not grand bargains. Additionally,‬‭track-two dialogues‬‭(unofficial talks involving‬
‭former officials, tribal leaders, or NGOs) can run in parallel to official channels. Such dialogues might‬
‭explore long-term issues – e.g. frameworks for a future political process – in a low-pressure setting,‬
‭feeding ideas back to official negotiators.‬
‭Throughout any engagement,‬‭legal and ethical standards‬‭must be upheld‬‭. Slovenia will insist that‬
‭engagement remain “principled.” This means continued condemnation of abuses even while talking, and‬
‭no actions that would violate international sanctions or laws. For example, any financial transactions as‬
‭part of engagement must comply with anti-terrorism financing rules. The UNSC can support the U.N.’s‬
‭role as a mediator: giving UNAMA a strong mandate to liaise with the de facto authorities on behalf of‬
‭the international community. Notably, in late 2023 the Council called for the U.N. Secretary-General to‬
‭develop a roadmap for dialogue‬‭– a process to outline‬‭what the Taliban must do to eventually earn‬
‭international acceptance​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. Engaging the Taliban also involves regional players: countries like Pakistan, China, Iran, and Russia‬
‭have more direct influence as they kept their embassies in Kabul. Slovenia can encourage these states to‬
‭use their channels to press the Taliban on shared concerns (for instance, Pakistan on counterterrorism, Iran‬
‭on refugee flows, etc.), all while coordinating with Western states. The balance Slovenia seeks is‬‭“critical‬
‭engagement”‬‭– talk to the Taliban to avert suffering‬‭and conflict, but‬‭with no hint of recognition until‬
‭they meet fundamental international norms‬‭​‬
‭aa.com.tr‬
‭. By walking this line, the UNSC can keep Afghanistan on the agenda and possibly nudge the Taliban‬
‭toward reforms, without abandoning the Afghan people or endorsing an oppressive regime.‬
‭Committee Plan for Slovenia (Short-Term vs. Long-Term)‬
‭As a member of the Security Council,‬‭Slovenia’s plan‬‭is to pursue a dual-track approach: address‬
‭immediate humanitarian and human rights crises in the short term, while laying groundwork for‬
‭sustainable improvements and engagement in the long term. This approach respects Slovenia’s stance of‬
‭non-recognition of the Taliban and focuses on tangible help for Afghans.‬
‭Short-Term Strategies (Immediate Actions)‬
‭●‬ ‭Humanitarian Surge:‬‭Slovenia will urge the UNSC and‬‭U.N. members to mount an immediate‬
‭humanitarian surge. This includes‬‭fully funding U.N.‬‭appeals‬‭and possibly organizing an‬
‭emergency donor conference to plug funding gaps. Slovenia can propose a UNSC‬‭resolution or‬
‭statement calling for unhindered humanitarian access‬‭,‬‭explicitly demanding the Taliban‬
‭remove barriers like the ban on women aid workers. The goal is to get food, medical supplies, and‬
‭shelter to those most in need before the next winter. Slovenia also supports innovative delivery‬
‭methods – for example,‬‭using the World Food Programme’s‬‭air bridges‬‭or pre-positioning‬
‭supplies in neighboring countries for quick transport into Afghanistan. In line with this, Slovenia‬
‭will highlight the plight of returnees and refugees; it supports increased U.N. assistance to Afghan‬
‭refugees in Iran and Pakistan, which relieves pressure on Afghanistan itself​‬
‭reporting.unhcr.org‬
‭.‬
‭●‬ ‭Protecting Women and Girls:‬‭Diplomatically, Slovenia‬‭will make Afghanistan’s women a‬
‭central theme of Council discussions. In the short term, that means leading on statements that‬
‭condemn the latest Taliban decrees and‬‭demand access‬‭to education and work for women‬‭.‬
‭Slovenia can initiate an emergency UNSC‬‭press statement‬‭or meeting focused exclusively on‬
‭women’s rights in Afghanistan‬‭, ensuring the issue‬‭stays in the international spotlight. It will‬
‭also support the renewal and strengthening of‬‭UNAMA’s‬‭mandate to monitor human rights‬
‭and report on abuses against women​‬
‭buildingtrust.si‬
‭. Concurrently, Slovenia will work with partner states to amplify Afghan women’s voices – for‬
‭instance, arranging for Afghan women activists to brief the Council (even if only via video from‬
‭exile, given many cannot speak freely at home). By keeping global attention on gender apartheid‬
‭in Afghanistan, Slovenia aims to pressure the Taliban to rethink their most draconian policies.‬
‭●‬ ‭No Recognition, But Active Engagement:‬‭In the short‬‭term, Slovenia will‬‭refuse any move‬
‭toward recognizing the Taliban regime‬‭. However, it‬‭will encourage‬‭pragmatic engagement‬
‭through the U.N. framework. Slovenia supports the U.N.’s‬‭“Doha format” talks‬‭that bring‬
‭together international envoys and Taliban officials in an informal setting​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭. Slovenia could offer to participate or provide expertise in these talks, particularly on‬
‭humanitarian logistics or human rights benchmarks. Importantly, Slovenia will coordinate with‬
‭the EU to ensure a unified message: the Taliban must earn any legitimacy through actions, not‬
‭words​‬
‭aa.com.tr‬
‭. Short-term engagement will focus on‬‭confidence-building‬‭measures‬‭– e.g. advocating for the‬
‭Taliban to allow polio vaccination campaigns countrywide, or to cooperate on locating and‬
‭clearing landmines. These are apolitical issues where cooperation could save lives and build a‬
‭modicum of trust.‬
‭●‬ ‭Leverage Frozen Assets for Aid:‬‭An immediate economic‬‭measure Slovenia champions is‬
‭unlocking frozen Afghan funds for humanitarian use. Many countries hold Afghan central bank‬
‭assets frozen since 2021​‬
‭hrw.org‬
‭. Slovenia proposes that the UNSC‬‭authorize a mechanism‬‭(possibly through a U.N. trust fund)‬
‭to use a portion of those funds to purchase critical supplies – grain, medicines, power generators –‬
‭which would be delivered directly to Afghanistan’s people under U.N.‬
‭supervision​file-5qtbsnewp7oqv1u5ouacvj. This would inject resources to alleviate suffering‬
‭without handing cash to the Taliban. Such an initiative could be time-bound and reviewed‬
‭regularly. In parallel, Slovenia will encourage international financial institutions to‬‭offer basic‬
‭technical support‬‭to Afghanistan (for example, helping‬‭maintain the electricity grid or drought‬
‭mitigation) under monitoring, so that humanitarian infrastructure does not completely erode.‬
‭●‬ ‭Diplomatic Coordination:‬‭In the UNSC, Slovenia will work closely with both Western allies‬
‭and regional powers to keep consensus. This means consulting with countries like China, Russia,‬
‭and India – who have stakes in Afghan stability – to find common ground on humanitarian‬
‭objectives even if political views diverge. Slovenia can use its bridging capacity as an EU‬
‭member that also engages with non-Western states to craft resolutions that all can support (e.g.‬
‭emphasizing aid and counterterrorism, which everyone agrees on). In the short term, a concrete‬
‭diplomatic step could be a‬‭UNSC presidential statement‬‭(which requires unanimity) reaffirming‬
‭support for Afghanistan’s people, calling for women’s rights, and underscoring that the Council’s‬
‭measures (sanctions, etc.) are not intended to harm civilians. Securing such a statement with all‬
‭15 members – including those typically sympathetic to the Taliban – would be a notable‬
‭achievement in unity.‬
‭Long-Term Strategies (Sustainable Solutions)‬
‭●‬ ‭Conditional Engagement Roadmap:‬‭Slovenia envisions‬‭the development of a‬‭long-term‬
‭roadmap‬‭for engaging any Afghan authorities, tied‬‭strictly to benchmarks. In the UNSC,‬
‭Slovenia will support the U.N. Secretary-General’s effort to create a‬‭“pathway to recognition”‬
‭document‬‭– essentially a list of conditions and steps‬‭the Taliban (or any future Afghan‬
‭government) must meet to gain gradual acceptance​‬
‭aa.com.tr‬
‭aa.com.tr‬
‭. These conditions would include forming a more inclusive government, upholding fundamental‬
‭human rights (especially for women and minorities), renouncing terrorism, and respecting‬
‭international law. The process would lay out what the international community would offer in‬
‭return for each major step (for example, the sequence might be: reopen secondary schools for‬
‭girls‬‭nationwide‬‭, then certain sanctions are lifted‬‭or development projects resume). This‬
‭approach gives the Taliban a clear choice and timeline, and it keeps international engagement‬
‭principled over the long run. Slovenia would contribute its expertise in international law to ensure‬
‭the roadmap’s benchmarks align with global norms and Slovenia’s values.‬
‭●‬ ‭Sustainable Economic Development:‬‭For the long term,‬‭Slovenia will promote strategies aimed‬
‭at moving Afghanistan from dependency to self-reliance –‬‭but only if governance improves‬‭. A‬
‭key part of this is regional economic integration. Slovenia, through the EU and U.N., can‬
‭facilitate dialogue on including Afghanistan in regional trade initiatives like the‬‭Central‬
‭Asia-South Asia power project (CASA-1000)‬‭or transport‬‭corridors linking Central Asia to‬
‭South Asia. In Council discussions, Slovenia can highlight projects such as‬‭railways connecting‬
‭Uzbekistan and Pakistan via Afghanistan‬‭, or expanding‬‭Iran’s Chabahar port access for‬
‭Afghan trade​‬
‭press.un.org‬
‭, as future opportunities if stability returns. The idea is to give Afghans a stake in a peaceful,‬
‭law-abiding future economy. Likewise, tapping Afghanistan’s vast mineral resources (copper,‬
‭lithium, rare earths) could greatly benefit the country, but Slovenia will insist this must be done‬
‭transparently and with protections in place – perhaps under U.N. or multilateral development‬
‭bank oversight – to ensure profits help the Afghan people and not just a few. Long-term, once‬
‭basic conditions are met, Slovenia would support the‬‭resumption of development aid‬‭and‬
‭investment in Afghanistan’s infrastructure (roads, schools, clean water, renewable energy) to lift‬
‭the country out of protracted crisis. Any such aid would be conditional on inclusivity – for‬
‭instance, infrastructure projects should hire local labor including women, and education aid must‬
‭include girls’ schooling.‬
‭●‬ ‭Human Rights Mechanisms:‬‭Slovenia will work to institutionalize‬‭human rights oversight for‬
‭the long haul. This includes continuing the mandate of the U.N. Special Rapporteur on‬
‭Afghanistan and potentially establishing a‬‭Commission‬‭of Inquiry‬‭or strengthening the role of‬
‭the International Criminal Court regarding Afghanistan if crimes against humanity (like gender‬
‭persecution) continue. While accountability may not come swiftly, documenting abuses now‬
‭builds the case for future justice. Slovenia’s commitment to‬‭Responsibility to Protect (R2P)‬
‭principles means it will remind the UNSC that the international community has a duty to protect‬
‭populations from mass atrocity crimes​‬
‭file-eflmh2daug3ysqcva697un‬
‭. If the situation in Afghanistan were to further deteriorate into widespread atrocity (for example,‬
‭targeted violence against an ethnic group or mass famine inflicted by policy), Slovenia would‬
‭advocate for R2P discussions – though any action would require careful international‬
‭deliberation. In the long term, improving human rights also involves Afghan civil society. Thus,‬
‭Slovenia will push for‬‭programs that support Afghan‬‭civil society actors, journalists, and‬
‭women’s groups‬‭, even if they must operate from exile‬‭for now. The UNSC can encourage U.N.‬
‭agencies to fund educational and leadership programs for Afghan women and youth (e.g.‬
‭scholarships abroad, regional training) so that an entire generation is not lost. These investments‬
‭in people are part of a long-term bet on Afghanistan’s future beyond the current regime.‬
‭●‬ ‭Future Diplomatic Framework:‬‭Recognizing that the‬‭Taliban’s hold on power may evolve,‬
‭Slovenia supports exploring a‬‭future political settlement‬‭in Afghanistan‬‭. In the long run,‬
‭stability may require an internal dialogue among Afghans – including the Taliban, other political‬
‭factions, ethnic leaders, and the diaspora – to chart a more inclusive governance structure. While‬
‭this is ultimately for Afghans to decide, the U.N. can facilitate when the time is ripe. Slovenia‬
‭would back a U.N.-led‬‭peace process or loya jirga‬‭(grand assembly)‬‭format if moderate‬
‭elements emerge or if there is internal push for a new constitutional order. In preparation,‬
‭Slovenia will engage with Afghanistan’s neighbors and major powers to form a‬‭contact group‬
‭that can swiftly support any nascent peace efforts. The long-term diplomatic vision is to‬
‭reintegrate a reformed Afghanistan into the international community – including eventually‬
‭returning an accredited government to the U.N. seat – but only after it adheres to international‬
‭standards. Until then, Slovenia will maintain the principled stance of‬‭“help the Afghan people,‬
‭pressure the Taliban regime.”‬‭This balanced approach‬‭in the Council keeps hope alive that‬
‭Afghanistan’s crisis can one day be resolved through sustained international support and‬
‭Afghan-led change.‬
‭By combining these short-term and long-term strategies, Slovenia aims to address immediate suffering‬
‭while not losing sight of Afghanistan’s future. This comprehensive plan ensures that in all Security‬
‭Council deliberations, Slovenia will advocate for the Afghan people’s welfare and rights, insist on‬
‭conditions for the Taliban’s engagement, and contribute to a unified international approach to one of the‬
‭world’s most challenging crises. Through steadfast commitment to its values – human rights, peace, and‬
‭development – Slovenia will help steer the Council toward actions that alleviate the humanitarian crisis‬
‭today and foster a more stable, inclusive Afghanistan tomorrow.‬
